items.title: Jerry Dodgion interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996
items.q: Well in the saxophones there’s Frank Wess and Dick Oatts, Ralph LaLama, Gary Smulyan. Slide Hampton’s in the band and he writes for the band too which is —

ctx.x: Talk to him, yeah. Who else is playing in that group?
Well in the saxophones there’s Frank Wess and Dick Oatts, Ralph LaLama, Gary Smulyan. Slide Hampton’s in the band and he writes for the band too which is —
We know that. We heard that the other night.

items.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010
items.q: when I was subbing, it was Pepper Adams, you know Jerry Dodgion, you know what I mean? All these guys.

ctx.x: You said something yesterday, you said you learned more on that gig on the first few weeks than you did in college. What do you learn on that first — I mean what was so memorable?

Well just what the thing sounded like around you. You know, and how they handled, I mean these were masters of playing jazz music. And I’m just out of college. And Tony Leonardi was great, believe me, I mean I learned a lot from him. But now this is experiencing it. That’s what I mean. Even with now you say about the band with Thad and Mel or the Mel Lewis band, that was more like real life. I mean he dealt with a lot — you know it’s in your home town which is now New York, you go to work and just the music was…
That’s okay. I like long answers. I don’t know if I can phrase this question correctly, but in improvisation, in jazz improvisation, to you, what constitutes a wrong note?
